Is the government able to give us any information in regard to the strike at Thetford Mines?

Mr. Speaker, the first information received by the government in regard to this
strike was this morning in a letter from the correspondent of the department at Thetford Mines. The strike appears to have started on Monday morning, some four hundred men being concerned. subsubtopic: UNITED STATES SCHOONER SILOAM FIRED ON BY PROTECTION STEAMER MALASPINA
speechtext: Can the government give us any information with respect to the killing of two American citizens by the crew of a Canadian patrol boat off Vancouver Island yesterday?

speakeroldname: Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Marine and Fisheries):
subsubtopic: UNITED STATES SCHOONER SILOAM FIRED ON BY PROTECTION STEAMER MALASPINA
speechtext:
A preliminary report has been prepared in connection with this incident. Here is what has been supplied to me:
The fishery protection steamer Malaspina, Captain Newcombe in command, sighted the United States schooner Siloam, of Seattle, engaged in fishing within one mile of Solander island. Upon sighting the schooner, the captain blew three whistles, the usual signal for the schooner to stop. No attention having been paid this signal, the Malaspina fired three blank shots across the bow of the schooner. The latter continuing, two solid shots were fired across the

French Treaty

bow, but still no attention from the schooner. The captain of the Malaspina at this point hailed the captain of the schooner again, requesting him to stop, but he declined to do so. Two solid shots were then fired but missed, after which the Malaspina demanded that the schooner stop, warning the captain that if these instructions were not obeyed the vessel would be sunk. The schooner persisted in paying no attention to this warning, consequently no alternative was left to the captain of the Malaspina but to fire a rifle volley at the pilot house.
Unfortunately a man was wounded, but the schooner stopped and the schooner's boat brought the wounded man to the Malaspina and then headed for the shore. The report continues.
The Malaspina lowered a boat at once and a line was put on board the schooner, when it was discovered that the crew had scuttled her before leaving. The Malaspina then endeavoured to tow her, although full of water, and obtain medical aid for the wounded man. The Mounted Police and other authorities were notified and tried to arrest the four other men of the schooner's crew who had escaped.
It is the opinion of the officers of the department that these men are not American citizens, though they were on an American schooner; they are probably foreigners. We will have a final and more complete report in a short time.

A number of papers in the United States and Canada are calling attention to the conditions which exist with regard to the rum running traffic. It is claimed that Canada is being used as a base for this illicit traffic from this country to the United States, and further that the new regulations are not at all effective in preventing this evil. I should like to ask whether the government is bringing in any measures with a view to dealing effectively with this matter?

French Treaty

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: BILL TO RATIFY-DEBATE ON SECOND READING CONCLUDED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to continue, though I fear my remarks will have to be brief, the discussion of the second reading of the French Treaty Bill. At the last sitting I called attention to the valuable concessions this country had given, concessions that aggregated a loss in revenue unquestionably amounting to between half a million and a million dollars-revenue that was derived from the users of undoubted luxuries and now must be made up by taking more or declining to take less from the pockets of the users of undoubted necessities. The price we pay does not end there. The price we pay involves as well disabilities upon primary producers of this country, producers of wines, producers, or contemplated and quite practical producers, of silks and many commodities in respect of which we now have remaining little more than a nominal duty against the importation. Every single item that appears in the schedules of the treaty affecting goods coming to Canada is a real item; every one is an item of some importance; many of them are items of major importance. The French negotiators did not consider that printer's ink was of particular value in a treaty; they wanted concessions that were concessions, and they got them. They did not think of the wisdom of going back to their parliament with a long list of articles which eve'n their parliament would know nothing about, such as was the course pursued by our representatives.
I want now to dwell on what we obtain which is alleged to be of value in the treaty; and I will not need to be detailed at all. The hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Chaplin) has placed upon Hansard figures taken from our export and import returns that bear directly on the value of this treaty on both sides, on the value of every concession or of everything that is supposed to be a concession to us. All that has been said about the treaty, assuming everything the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) has uttered to be correct, does not shatter in the least degree the case made by the* hon. member for Lincoln. The Minister of Finance says, "Oh, we get concessions here in respect of certain goods asked to be reduced by the Canadian Manufacturers' Association," and he read a list of those goods, undoubtedly articles in respect of which he has already had the duty reduced down to the
American level, in some cases down to the minimum tariff, but in all cases to the American level, and he says: Look at that for a triumph! Is not that something worth while? Those articles, he says, are not to be treated with scorn as the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Chaplin) treated them. Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Lincoln treated no article that the minister mentioned with scorn, not at all. He admitted they were concessions. But are they of much value? Surely ministers do not come here and say they sat for three, four or five months in Paris trying to get a few spare parts of implements down to the American level of duty.
Take the minister's speech and read the articles to which he attributes so much importance-certain portions of agricultural implements, canvass for binders, magnetos for another implement that we sell to France, that is for automobiles, and other articles of similar kind. Read the list from beginning to end and I venture to say that there is not one article that the French people would not readily have reduced to the American level in their own interests for reasons that are so obvious that we would not need to send anybody to France. These articles are binder canvasses, canvass straps, magnetos, ordinary cast iron spares, straight solid steel shafts, tubular bored straight shafts, spark plugs and certain articles of a similar character in iron and steel. The French people are using the completed products of these goods. They have our binders, our mowers, our automobiles, and they found they could not get these spare parts except over a prohibitive duty. Why, the French people, one would think, would be at the door of their government to have these articles reduced. But it is worth something to Canada. No one disputes that it is of some value to the manufacturers of these goods, and they would ask for it, but it is no triumph for the Canadian negotiators and no real concession on the part of France. Grant the reduced duties on these articles, and everything the Minister of Finance has mentioned, and in sight of that meagre array just let us bring to our minds what the Minister of Finance has given.
I will refer in a moment to the contention of the minister that he could not do any better, that he did the best he could. But it is surely worth while for us to compare the conditions under this treaty with the conditions that existed before. If it is not, then the Minister of Finance simply raises the white flag and he says: We have got to do what ("very high tariff country in this world tells us; we have to do it; we have to bow-down and submit to the exactions which any
French Treaty

country wishes to impose. If the treaty we have with them is not good enough for them and they want something more to their advantage, all they have to do is to say so. That on the plea that he could do no better is the position of the Minister of Finance.
No, Mr. Speaker, we must compare the conditions under this treaty with the conditions that existed before, and I say that we would be infinitely better off without this treaty and have the conditions that existed before; and if France wants to get rid of the conditions that existed before, surely we are not going to proclaim that we are absolutely without weapons while France has all the weapons in her hands.	[DOT]
The minister has his schedule A in respect of which he has the French minimum tariff. Well, the French minimum tariff may be of value on certain goods, and may be of no value at all on other goods, and I venture to say that the Minister of Finance has not secured one single reduction in respect of schedule A, his best schedule, that is of any substantial value to the Dominion of Canada. But it is his best schedule. Most of our exports are under that schedule, the body of our exports that go to France to-day are under the general tariff, the general tariff being as regards them the same as the minimum tariff. Surely the minister was not afraid that there would be a penalty duty imposed against Canada. Our wheat, our grain and all these things that we export in tremendous quantities do not go very much into France, it is true, because the duty is so high, but they are our chief exports. The French general tariff is the same on them as their minimum tariff, and on the first page of Schedule A which embraces 65 per cent of the exports of Canada, the minister has secured reductions on five articles not one dollar of which we ever send to France, and the exports of Canada in relation to all of them and the possibilities of exports, well, they are almost negligible. They amount to nothing at all. Relative to the trade of the nation they are merely chicken feed, and the same applies to page 2 and page 3 of schedule A. The minister has nothing for this country on these pages. Go over , them one after the other. I think the total number of articles that come after page 1 of schedule A on which the minister has secured reductions is 19, and you can go over them one after another and you will rind in nearly all cases, and in all cases of consequence, that we are buyers of the same' goods from France or from the world, and in many cases from France herself, buyers in large amounts, and not exporters at all. Where we are exporters it is in trifling sums, (Mr. Meishen.]
and very little or nothing to France. Now what value is such a schedule to this country? Is it worth while paying an annual sum of from five hundred thousand to a million dollars for? Is it so worth while when we must throw down our bars on luxuries to Japan, to Italy, to Switzerland and all of some eleven favoured nations?

subsubtopic: BILL TO RATIFY-DEBATE ON SECOND READING CONCLUDED
speechtext:
Does the right hon.
leader of the Opposition mean to* infer that it is an expense to the Canadian people to get goods at a lower cost?

subsubtopic: BILL TO RATIFY-DEBATE ON SECOND READING CONCLUDED
speechtext:
Yes I do, when we have to pay extra on goods that we need far more. I wonder if the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) was in the Liberal convention in which they solemnly resolved to tax luxuries? He was there. Now he is going to support a bill which reduces the tax on luxuries and consequently imposes a heavier tax on necessaries. That is what I am against.
Now leaving schedule A, which is the best schedule, we have nothing at all that compares with the concessions granted-nothing at all. I venture to say, Mr. Speaker, that in respect to schedule B there are at least twenty-five penalties imposed on us the injury to Canada as regards any one of which is greater than all that we get in the whole of schedule A. In schedule B there are thirty articles, our large exports many of them, exports of which we send a substantial quantity to France, in respect of which the minister has gone over and yielded to the demand of France for a far higher duty than existed before. I say again, you can take not all of them upon which the tariff against us is raised by this treaty-there are about three not of very great consequence, but not more than three-there are twenty-five at any rate that are of outstanding consequence, and all of them or nearly all are of consequence to the agricultural producers of Canada. Is this the way to get wider markets? How are hon. gentlemen who are down here on a crusade for wider markets going to go h^me to their constituencies and say: The first vote I had on any treaty for wider markets I cast to curtail and contract the markets for the agricultural products of our country, but I did it because the Minister of Finance told me that when another country had a higher tariff than we had, we simply had to do it and that if we. pursued a low tariff doctrine, the same thing is what we would have to do every time. Such is the answer they will hat e to make, to their constituents as to why they voted for this contraction of the agricultural products markets of this country. The hon.

French Treaty
member for Brome shakes his head. Does he not see in this treaty agricultural products and manufactures of agricultural products one by one to at least twenty with the French duty raised against them, and he cannot point to one agricultural product with the duty lowered? Now he shakes his head; let him speak.

subsubtopic: BILL TO RATIFY-DEBATE ON SECOND READING CONCLUDED
speechtext: Exactly.

subsubtopic: BILL TO RATIFY-DEBATE ON SECOND READING CONCLUDED
speechtext: We cannot help but bow in admiration before the optimism of the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster). Yes, in every respect the farmers, through this treaty, have barriers put up against, them. They have had to submit to the erection of higher barriers against the sale of the agricultural products of this country; against poultry, against meats, against potatoes, against vegetables, against condensed milk, against stock, against the main agricultural exports of Canada save grain alone. In respect of grain they have the general tariff of France and nothing more. In respect of live animals we have not yet succeeded in selling any to France.

subsubtopic: BILL TO RATIFY-DEBATE ON SECOND READING CONCLUDED
speechtext: Any what?

subsubtopic: BILL TO RATIFY-DEBATE ON SECOND READING CONCLUDED
speechtext:
Any live animals. As regards those we have a higher tariff even than we had before. The possibility of widening our markets for stock in France is Stopped.
If we could not sell any in the face of a tariff of 20 francs, we are not likely to sell any in the face of a tariff of 21i francs. In other cases we have to face a duty of 100 per cent more than we previously had; and a duty of 50 per cent more is frequently found in this new French tariff. And this is what we are asked to submit to. We are asked to take this because-in the words of the Finance Minister-after five months' work he could not for the life of him get anything better. Now, I want hon. gentlemen to reflect upon our position in that regard. The Canadian ministers had, in order to maintain that this is a low tariff country, in order to save the face of the Minister of Finance-who has been preaching low tariff in opposition and binding himself to general reductions every time he got on his feet-they had to curtail and contract the export market for the agricultural products of Canada. What a fine confession to make to the agricultural producers of this country. I can imagine the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries sitting beside the statesmen of France negotiating this treaty as one by one these articles were produced. Condensed milk was laid before the Minister of Finance and he was told, " You will have to submit to 50 per cent more duty, half as much again, on this; you will have to submit to a higher duty on live stock; you will have to submit to a duty of half as much again, or more, on meats and vegetables of which we export large amounts representing a value of millions ". The minister, I fancy, protested, and kept on protesting-for five months, but the French negotiators sat there with the Liberal platform in their pockets. They had the Liberal convention report, they had the resolution moved by the minister himself iu this House, and they said to him, " What do you propose to do if we increase these duties?"; -and the minister could not say that he would raise the tariff against French luxuries imported into this country. If he did they would laugh at him. He could not even protest against higher duties on articles going into France. The French negotiators would say to him, "You have been arguing in your parliament for years that the putting up of duties by us only hurts ourselves" and so he could not complain; he did not have a word to say for himself. All the French negotiators needed to have was simply the record of the speeches of the Minister of Finance in this parliament, the record of his resolutions, and they would be still better armed with a copy of that precious document the report of the Liberal convention of 1919. Faced with these things the minister was helpless, and that is
French Treaty

why he is back to this House with this treaty. But is his quandary any reason why we should accept the treaty? Is it any-reason why this House should accept this humiliating surrender which the Minister of Finance proposes to us? This is a capitulation-in every line of the treaty it is a capitulation to France. In many respects it is a bigger capitulation to Japan from whom we get nothing at all than it is to France; a bigger capitulation to Switzerland, in many respects, than it is to France. All this we are asked to take from the Minister of Finance on the mere plea that he could not do any better, when we know the reason he could not do any better was his own insincere conduct in opposition. For his conduct this country is now paying the penalty in the form of this treaty.
Will the minister suggest to me anything, save those things that he gets under Schedule A, that is of value to this country? I do not know of anything that he gets that is of value anyway to the agriculturists of Canada. He does get something that is better in respect to certain manufactured products which I have named; but even in getting them he does not secure any concession from France which could not have been secured with far less trouble and infinitely less sacrifice on the part of the government of Canada.
I want again to inquire why the Minister of Finance comes to this parliament with an illusion, a grotesque pact-a poor, helpless treaty, surrounded and buried in pure padding? "Oh," he says, "We may make some of these things some day." Is that a real excuse for having these articles in the treaty? I turn the minister's attention to a page and a half containing over one hundred articles, page 21 and half of 22, and I take the chance of saying to the minister now that he cannot tell me what one of those articles is. I will go further. I venture to suggest that there is not a member of the government that has the faintest idea what one out of those one hundred articles is at all. I admit that I do not, and I do not know where to find out.

subsubtopic: BILL TO RATIFY-DEBATE ON SECOND READING CONCLUDED
speechtext:
How could anybody
else expect to know if the minister does not?

subsubtopic: BILL TO RATIFY-DEBATE ON SECOND READING CONCLUDED
speechtext:
Maybe the member for Brome would and for the purpose of this inquiry, although not for any other purpose, I will include him as a member of the government-will he give the information to this House? All this was done simply to cover the surrender of our interests that the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries made in their negotiations; it was done simply to cover up the surrender of our real interests under this copious pact

of page after page of articles the nature of which none of us know and the names of which we cannot even pronounce. I invite any member of this House to take some of these products with names of thirty or forty letters and practise for half a day the pronouncing of them. I conjecture the result would be that nobody could tell what he was saying. This is a feature of the treaty we have entered into.

subsubtopic: BILL TO RATIFY-DEBATE ON SECOND READING CONCLUDED
speechtext: The value of a pharmacopoeia does not depend upon its pronun-ciability.

subsubtopic: BILL TO RATIFY-DEBATE ON SECOND READING CONCLUDED
speechtext: Will the hon. member tell me the value of even one of these one hundred articles. On the authority of the best chemist we can find-

subsubtopic: BILL TO RATIFY-DEBATE ON SECOND READING CONCLUDED
speechtext: Dr. Sheard?

subsubtopic: BILL TO RATIFY-DEBATE ON SECOND READING CONCLUDED
speechtext:
-we are assured that none of them was ever made in this country. In a letter that was read to the House at the last session the best chemist in the country stated that although these products are made in some other land none of them was ever produced in Canada save one and that the ingredients for this one exception all had to be imported. Yet this is supposed to be a treaty. But the matter is serious. In respect of real exports from Canada it is very serious. We are going to suffer a handicap from the day this treaty goes into effect onward because of the surrender of the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries; and all we have to weigh is, whether the reasons for the surrender were such that we should now accept this treaty as part of the inevitable. That is all we have to weigh. Nobody disputes that we are injured by this treaty. The Minister of Finance himself in his speech says that the French people were not willing to compete with us as favourably as they were back in 1907 when he made his previous treaty.
There was a temporary extension of the 1907 treaty with some alterations in 1921-a very good extension under all the circumstances. This was in effect when the Minister of Finance went over, and he said France was not ready to treat on so favourable a basis as in that, which is another way of admitting that he has brought back worse conditions than he took over. There is no use labouring the matter further, but I venture to say any hon. member of this House who will examine the schedules and our exports will place a far greater value upon what this country loses by the treaty than did the Minister of Finance.

French Treaty
But he says we have secured on some articles the schedules already accorded the United States. Now I do not dispute-and the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Chaplin) did not dispute-that this was worth something, but is it something for which we should make large-very large-concessions to France? Why, let me ask, should we be penalized by France as between ourselves and the United States of America? I should like hon. members to reflect on that and try to answer. Does any hon. member know why the United States should enjoy, for no concession whatever, for no pretence of a concession, in the face of a policy that definitely denies a concession, something that Canada can only secure by granting heavy concessions? Would it be much of a triumph if the Minister of Finance had come back with equal conditions as between this country and the United States in the tariff of France? I do not think it would. But that he has not obtained-not by a very long way. The United States are not letting silks, embroideries, satins, brandies and champagnes, and all these other products into their country, the way we are doing in Canada. They are not imposing taxes on necessaries in order that they may relieve the consumers of luxuries. They are not doing such things in order to get, as they do get, everything we are getting by this treaty.
I wish to refer to another phase. When we grant to France the right to send her silks to Canada at a certain rate of duty, we grant the same thing to eleven favoured nations, with the result that in case after case we are making far more concessions to the other countries than we are making to France herself.

subsubtopic: BILL TO RATIFY-DEBATE ON SECOND READING CONCLUDED
speechtext: Does that hurt France?

subsubtopic: BILL TO RATIFY-DEBATE ON SECOND READING CONCLUDED
speechtext: Undoubtedly it does- and it hurts us. It merely puts more taxes on the users of necessaries in our country. If it does not hurt Canada, if it helps Canada, why leave any tariff on? That is where the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) is, but not where the Minister of Finance stands. Who is going t-o argue that it is a benefit to us to maintain our taxes on necessaries and reduce our taxes on luxuries? The supporter of this treaty is bound so to maintain, or to admit, that we make very serious concessions for worse than nothing.

subsubtopic: BILL TO RATIFY-DEBATE ON SECOND READING CONCLUDED
speechtext: Why could we not collect some of our taxes in some other way than by transferring the duties from luxuries to necessaries?

subsubtopic: BILL TO RATIFY-DEBATE ON SECOND READING CONCLUDED
speechtext:
I think the Minister of
Finance will have to do just that. But the
hon. member for Brant (Mr. Good) must remember that last year the way he increased taxes was chiefly by a 50 per cent increase in the sales tax, which came on everybody. Does the member for Brant hope to reduce the sales tax by relieving the users of luxuries of their taxes? Indeed he does not. He shakes his head honestly in the negative. If we do not get an increased sales tax this year, to make up what we are losing under this, or if we do not get a reduction when we should otherwise get it, it is because of the blunders of the concessions of this treaty, and he who votes for the treaty votes to shut the door on the reduction of our sales tax, and he votes to shut the door against relief on the necessaries of life. Of course the Minister of Finance knows that just to the extent this treaty operates that is what he is doing.

subsubtopic: BILL TO RATIFY-DEBATE ON SECOND READING CONCLUDED
speechtext: Not necessarily.

subsubtopic: BILL TO RATIFY-DEBATE ON SECOND READING CONCLUDED
speechtext: What is the plan proposed by the hon. member for Brome?

subsubtopic: BILL TO RATIFY-DEBATE ON SECOND READING CONCLUDED
speechtext:
I think, perhaps, the
leader of the Opposition might realize that even in silks the reduction of duty might mean increased imports, and might mean greater revenue raised.

subsubtopic: BILL TO RATIFY-DEBATE ON SECOND READING CONCLUDED
speechtext:
It might, but the Minister of Finance himself estimates that it will be $S50,000 less. In any event I am not quite able to understand just how this country is going to get richer or pay debts faster by buying more silks and champagnes or buying more of anything that is embraced in the schedules of the treaty where we make concessions to France.
I want to impress upon the House instances that go to show what we are actually doing when we sign this treaty. I call attention to the main exports of our country to France. Take them one by one from the largest until you get through, fifteen to twenty, and on each one you will find higher duties put up against us by France. Then take the imports of this country which compete with our own productions in some instances, and which in almost every instance are luxuries. Where we take the tariff off for the sake of France on goods she sells us of $100 value we sometimes take the tariff off Switzerland on goods she sells us of $300, $400, and even $1,000. That is a splendid way to make a concession to France, is it not? I have before me a list of the goods so affected, and I would like the House to bear with me while I call attention to some of them. I commence with braids and cords. We are lowering the duty to France, though she only sends us $46,000 worth odd, but we
French Treaty

are taking it off similarly to Switzerland, which country sends us $112,407, and Switzerland gives us nothing. It is true she does not pay us by raising the duty against us. I suppose from that point of view really Switzerland is better entitled to it than France. In respect of France, for doing this, we have the duty raised against us on our main imports to that country. In respect to Switzerland we do it for nothing at all. But let us pass on. In the matter of brushes, where France sells us $42,000 worth, Switzerland sells us $114,000 worth or about two and a half or three times as much, and we are making concessions on that article to Switzerland for nothing whatsoever. Going from that to buttons, where -we buy $11,000 worth from France we buy from Japan $107,000 worth, or nearly ten times as much, so that where we are making a concession of $1 to the French exporter to Canada, we are making a concession of $10 to the Japanese exporter to Canada. Will any hon. member tell me why we should do that? If we are bound to be making concessions on these lines of goods, we should have done two things first. We should have had a comparable tariff on them or, at least, a tariff from which we could have come down, and secondly we should have got rid of the necessity of making concessions to countries which give us nothing at all.

subsubtopic: BILL TO RATIFY-DEBATE ON SECOND READING CONCLUDED

subsubtopic: BILL TO RATIFY-DEBATE ON SECOND READING CONCLUDED

subsubtopic: BILL TO RATIFY-DEBATE ON SECOND READING CONCLUDED
speechtext: I will pass on, for I do not want to dwell too long on the infirmities of the hon. member. The next article is clocks and watches. Of these we import $3,829 worth from France, but from Switzerland we import $75,586 worth. For the sake of making a concession to France at our expense, we make virtually twenty-five times that concession to Switzerland.

subsubtopic: BILL TO RATIFY-DEBATE ON SECOND READING CONCLUDED
speechtext: Think of the saving of time.

subsubtopic: BILL TO RATIFY-DEBATE ON SECOND READING CONCLUDED
speechtext:
We did not save much
time in making this treaty. We lost about five months, and we also lost a great deal to this country. The next item is electrical apparatus, telephones and the like. Of these, whereas we bought from France $1,231 worth, we bought from Japan $18,000 odd worth, making about sixteen times the concession to Japan that we make to France, and all at the expense of this country.
The next item is embroideries. We buy $17,700 worth from France, and from Switzerland $100,598 worth. Of handkerchiefs we bought from France $5,000 odd worth, from Japan $77,000 odd worth, and from Switzerland

French Treaty
$225,000 odd worth; or hon. members will see that we bought some forty times as much from Switzerland as from France. We open our doors to all these countries with no concessions from them at all, and we also open them to France for the privilege of having the duties on our staple exports raised against us.
I could pass from one article to another, silk ribbons, toys, silk fabrics, various other things, some of them somewhat hard to pronounce, and in respect of every one of them we make many times the concession to favoured-nation countries that we 'have made to France.
Besides all this, we fix specific duties on our goods, duties that we cannot vary. This applies to quite a part of the treaty in relation to the duties of Canada. France does [DOT] not do so. We bind ourselves besides to maintain the same parity between our minimum tariff, and our general tariff as we have to-day. France makes no such covenant with us at all. Moreover, France has reserved the right-and there is no corresponding reservation for this country-to give to all neighbouring, as well as former enemy countries, all concessions that she gives to us. If she exercises that right, do hon. members know of anything that we can get in there under this treaty that will be of any value at all to Canadian exporters? Let her exercise that right in favour of all those neighbouring states, and she has cancelled or all but cancelled the meagre concessions that we already have. The ministers came back and they did not know the effect of that concession. When the matter was put to them in this House on the reading of the resolution, I think it was the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) who stated that this clause applied, as in previous treaties, just to a certain border zone, bordering on France. It is true that in previous treaties it applied only to such narrow border zone; but in this treaty there is no restriction at all. It applies to all the territory of all nations adjacent to France.
The hon. member for Chambly and Vercheres (Mr. Archambault) has argued-and I admire the ingenuity of the argument; I think he was driven to it-that he does not consider this treaty solely on an economic basis, and as a matter of dollars and cents. He says: "France suffered terriffic losses in the late war; she lost her million or two million men; she lost another two or three or more millions in disabilities. She lost as well tremendous amounts in property destruction. She sacrificed, of the very manhood and wealth of her nation, relatively more than any other nation that went through the war." In all that
I concur; but I do not think the hon. member for Chambly and Vercheres will say that I have at any time in my life shown anything but sympathy for and a real desire to help France in her struggle. I think I anticipate the character of campaign it is proposed to wage against those who question the desirability of this treaty. It seems to be disclosed in the speech of the hon. member; but they will have to direct it at all events against some hon. members who have in the crucial past done everything in their power and at considerable risk to render practical and needed assistance to France. I do not, however, believe in mixing up trade treaties with international obligations. It will be argued that we are under obligations to France greater than are the obligations of France to us. I do not admit that. This country sacrificed a great deal, and though we made the sacrifice for ourselves, we must remember that the direct peril to France was far greater than the direct peril to us. I do not admit there is a balance in favour of the other nation. I think we did our duty. We did not do any more; we would and should have done more if we could. That is quite true; but if there is an obligation, then I say: Let us in all honesty discharge it; but do not let us, in discharging it, pay a far greater sum to other countries to whom we are under no obligation whatever. If we seek that method of discharging a debt of honour, a debt of devotion to France, we are taking the most uneconomical, the most disastrous method to the interests of Canada and the 4 p.m. least beneficial to the interests of France. Far better, if there is an obligation, to discharge it in a direct way, in a way that we shall know just what we are doing, and not in a way that piles on the back of this country burdens far greater than the amount of the concession passing to France. France benefits by this treaty far more than we benefit; but other nations, benefit too, and while we are helping France we	are helping other nations,
nations to whom no one would argue that this country is under any obligation whatever. I do not yield even to the hon, member for Chambly and Vercheres in my admiration of the French character and the French nation, nor in my desire to assist in the rehabilitation of that country, stricken as it is, in the anguish of after-war collapse. But I do not believe that trade treaties are the right method, and I do not believe, if trade treaties are, that this is the character of treaty that we should make. I do not want to have included among our beneficiaries a number of countries to whom
French Treaty

we are under no obligation at all, Consequently I think we would be better to reject this treaty.
We are not without resources in this country. Surely hon. members will not argue that we have to sit down and take just what we get from countries that have a higher tariff level from our own. Surely hon. members will not argue that we must continue to do this ad infinitum and that we are utterly without resources to protect ourselves? But they must so argue if they ask us to support this treaty.
There are other courses we can take. France has something to lose by the rejection of this treaty; she stands to lose on exports that for the last fiscal year, of 1922, were far greater than her imports from us. Reject the treaty, adopt the resources that any self-respecting country would adopt and stand up in this battle with other nations. If we do not, we are only going to add to the distresses of our own. Every morning even now our newspapers are full of calamitous tales of our working men emigrating to the United States. As I came in I picked up the Liberal organ of the city of Montreal owned, or at least presided over, by a Liberal member of the Upper House, and I read the heading:
Montreal workmen going in thousands to United States-Present situation threatens serious labour shortage here-
Of course, solving the problem of unemployment triumphantly for the hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. Murdock).
Hundreds every day now storm offices of United States Immigration eager to cross the border-Recent immigrants join in.
And then proceeds the heartrending tale of what is going on. Is there anything in this treaty that is likely to deter one man from emigrating to the United States? Does not this treaty contain the germs that ultimately will result in more men going to the United States? I make this appeal particularly to the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler). Many phases of the concession mean that result, and that result alone.
Therefore I say this is not the course to pursue. Let us stand up and behave as a nation in our commercial as we would in all other negotiations, and not proclaim to the world that we must submit meekly and helplessly to the tariff exactions of any country.

Mr. Speaker, in beginning the discussion of this question this afternoon I propose to read a few words from an editorial in the Montreal Witness which came into my hand to-day as illustrating how hopelessly the people of Canada, as well as the members of this House, are divided on questions of trade in the way in which we look at treaties and tariffs. The editorial reads:
What is the use of discussion in parliament between men living in different worlds, who cannot even see each other's point of view, and perhaps don't want to The French Treaty, the protectionists argue, is all give and no take. On a lot of articles, such as tools, etc., they say Canada is to pay 50 per cent duty when she sends them into France, but it is only to collect 20 to 25 per cent on importing them from France. How would this read if we should put it this way? The French people have to pay 50 per cent duty on what they import as well as on ten times more that they do not import, while Canadians have to pay only 20 to 25 per cent. The trouble is that those on one side of the controversy can only see the protected interests, while those on the other keep the interests of the people who need tools somewhat in view.
It seems to me unfortunate that these treaties between nations are generally made an occasion for a very acrimonious controversy and the position is very frequently taken by the opponents of the government in power, whatever government it may be-and it seems to be the same in every country- that a treaty secured was not as good as it ought to be, and there has been a disposition to object to the treaty for that reason.
I was in the United States three years ago when the controversy was going on there as regards its attitude towards the League of Nations. I was at a meeting in the town of Waterbury, which by the way is a very strong Republican centre, and one man actually made the statement: "Now, that we have shown President Wilson where he gets off at, we want the treaty." They wanted the treaty, but they wanted and took the opportunity that was offered to them to get a slam at President Wilson. I do not think that principle has been entirely wanting in this country when we look over the past few years and 142
consider the situation in relation to the attempt to get trading arrangements with various nations. I would not like to say that it is absent on the present occasion. It seems to me that the most important question today is not: Did we get the best treaty possible? We do not know. Possibly those who negotiated the treaty, might, in their inmost souls, think that if they had been a little more firm on certain points they could have secured better terms. You can never tell when you are negotiating with a party just how far you can press him until negotiations come right to the breaking point. The most important question, at least for this parliament, to decide seems to be to-day whether, under this treaty, we are going to be placed in a better position than we would be in without the treaty. Notwithstanding the fact that hon. gentlemen to our right have declared positively that we would be better off without the treaty than we would be under circumstances that would prevail if we had the treaty, they have not made it clear to me that such is the case. When this treaty was first brought before the House, I was disposed to attach to it much the same valuation as I thought the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) attached to it in his speech in introducing it to us. Perhaps I drew inferences that were not altogether warranted on that occasion; but still in looking over the treaty and in giving a cursory glance at the schedules, I fail to find anything that would cause us to wax very enthusiastic. Speaking from the standpoint of those who are engaged in agriculture, I feel that as regards our major products, there does not seem to be in the treaty a great deal over which we could become enthusiastic. If there is in it the poison that the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) would seem to say there is, I would not want it; but on the principle that half a loaf is better than no bread, I for my part would be prepared to accept the treaty for what it is worth.
I will not deal very largely with the schedules in particular, but I should like to make a few comments as regards certain arguments that have been advanced why this treaty should not be accepted. Speaking generally, I think I can say, speaking, not only for myself, but for those with whom I am associated, that we are in favour of any attempt that can be made to break 5 p.m down the barriers which nations have erected amongst themselves in matters of trade. I would hope, therefore, that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell), who is not in his place, was not correctly re-

French Treaty

ported, or that he was misrepresented when he was reported to have said during the Moose Jaw campaign, that there was no evidence that the Progressives were not still opposed to reciprocity. If there is one thing that we have made abundantly clear in this House since we have been here, it is that we were strongly in favour of that reciprocity agreement. Perhaps the prominence given to that question in the Moose Jaw campaign ought to convince the country that the question of better trade relations with the United States is not dead; that it is alive, and that it is going to be very much alive. It might be well for those who were responsible for the rejection of that treaty, and those who are the political successors of those who rejected that treaty, to take cognizance of that fact. I know some explanations are given as to why they are in the position in which they are today. The hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) made a speech a short time ago in Winnipeg-and I suppose he repeated the same speech in Ottawa, because I know he said some of the same things here-stating that their party had sacrificed themselves because of the war. He seems to think that that was the reason of their present humiliation. When I read that statement, I wondered whether the sacrifice which they made was in being compelled to sit along with the hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion) and the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie). But seriously, speaking for the West and the prairie provinces only, I wish to say that it was not the war record or the post-war record of the hon. gentlemen that caused them to pass through the valley of humiliation. The people of the western prairies remembered 1911 and the kind of arguments that were foisted upon them at that time. When we remember the arguments that were put forward at that time, we are not disposed to attach too much value to the arguments that are advanced against this treaty to-day.
I said that T was not going to discuss in any great detail the schedules, but rather that I would make some comments upon arguments that have been advanced why we should reject the treaty. No doubt the arguments of hon. gentlemen are sound from their point of view, from the protectionist point of view, and if I belonged to that school, undoubtedly I would accept them as sound and consider it my duty to act in accordance with the sentiments they expressed. But since we have never accepted their point of view, and speak from an entirely different one, I cannot for one see how it is possible to respond to

the appeal that they have made. The hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Chaplin) advanced some arguments, and I have been somewhat amused at the way in which the shuttlecock has been batted backwards and forwards. I was disposed to think the weight of the argument lay with one side and then with the other; but I think at the present time the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Lapointe) has the advantage on his side.
The ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) laid a great deal of emphasis upon the question of the balance of trade. There seems to be some conflict in the figures that have been presented to us by the ex-Minister of Finance and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, and just at present I am not able to reconcile the two statements, although that may possibly be done. It seems to me, however, that many false conclusions have been based upon this question of an adverse balance of trade. It is by no means conclusive, by no means sure, as applied to trade as a whole, that an injury is necessarily done to a country because for the time being the balance would seem to be against it. But still less is it safe, when we come to consider relations between any two nations, to conclude that trade is necessarily detrimental to the one against which the balance would seem to be for the time being. International trade is not simply a two-sided question; it is not simply a case of A trading with B; it is a case of A trading with B, C, D and E, and B trading with all the rest of them. It is, therefore, absolutely impossible to establish conclusions as sound by considering simply the relations which for the time being exist between any two of those nations.
It has been urged that it would have been better if the government had raised the tariff before proceeding to enter into negotiations. That again is a principle of questionable soundness, even if we consider it in regard to our tariff as a whole, and still more questionable when we consider it in relation to this particular question. The right hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) has urged that the minister should have definitely increased the tariff against France on luxuries before entering into negotiations. I wonder how it would have been possible in that case for the ministers to have entered into negotiations at all. If it had been definitely stated in this House that in order to negotiate a trade bargain with France we would increase the tax upon luxuries, I can well imagine what response we would have had from the French people. The probability is our ministers would have come back without any treaty at

French Treaty
all. On the other hand, had it been definitely stated that luxuries would have to pay a higher tariff, I cannot see how it would have been possible to conclude such a treaty as this.
A great deal has been said about the most favoured nation clause. I again say that it cannot for a moment be contended that our ministers could have taken any other position in the negotiations. I maintain in regard to this treaty that negotiations should be entered upon in a spirit of good will and fairness towards other nations. It would seem to me impossible at this time to contend that we should continue to regard trade treaties in any other light than as arrangements of mutual advantage to the countries concerned. I cannot conceive, Mr. Speaker, that we should approach this question in any other spirit than that of a desire to make fair and equitable arrangements with those nations which are willing to trade with us.
A great deal of emphasis has been laid upon what is called the adverse balance of trade. It would seem to me to be absolutely unsound as between two nations that we should take a position based on this adverse balance of trade; at least it does not prove anything to my mind in this respect. Speaking generally, I would take the position that in all trade arrangements with other nations we must be willing to negotiate in a spirit of give and take; there must be no thought that we can retain all the advantage upon our own side. This treaty has been entered into with a nation that was our ally during the war, and it would ill become us to attempt to impose upon France obligations which, torn as she was by war, she might find it difficult to accept. Matters of trade should not, as in the past, be treated as, potentially, occasions of war, but rather as arrangements of mutual advantage to all concerned. We should always remember that trade is of paramount interest to all concerned, and that peace can only come in this world as we are willing to approach all nations in a spirit of good will.

But in any case I feel that I should support this bill and leave it to the intelligence and fair-mindedness of the Minister of Finance to right any wrong that might be occasioned, rather than vote against a measure which in other respects is, to my mind, of great advantage to the people of Canada.
The hon. member for Lincoln further staled that the treaty worked a great injustice to nursery men. He said:
I now wish to refer for a moment, but only in a general way, to some of the articles that France is allowed to sell Canada under this treaty. I would ask the Minister of Finance why shrubs, grape vines, gooseberry bushes, and trees of all kinds of which we have good growers in this country and of which we export considerable quantities are allowed to enter Canada at two cents apiece whereas similar provision has not been made for Canadian trees and shrubs on the part of France.
If my hon. friend will look at item 170 of the French tariff he will find that these articles go into France free of duty, so that the duty on nursery stock coming into Canada is to our advantage and not to the advantage of France.
The hon. member referred to a very large number of items, in connection with which he strove to show that the treaty was working a disadvantage. The right hon. leader of the Opposition also says that the existing treaty, which this convention does away with, is far better than the one we are now considering. He said also that the treaty of 1908 was still in force at the time this new convention was entered into and that it could have continued in force, and he read article 6 of the statute, as follows:
The present arrangement shall remain in force until the conclusion of a new commercial convention, but either of the high contracting parties may denounce it after four months' notice.
I think my right hon. friend was hardly fair in his criticism in regard to that matter, because he endeavoured to leave the impression on the members of this House and on the people throughout the country that the treaty of 1908 could have continued in force practically indefinitely. But the preamble, not of the act of 1920, but of the schedule to the act says:
Pending the conclusion of a new commercial convention, with a view to which negotiations will begin immediately, the French and Canadian governments have agreed to the following provisions.
So that whether intentionally or not, the right hon. gentleman was rather misleading

the House and the people when he suggested that the treaty could have remained in force for any considerable length of time.	.
Now, Sir, what do we find in regard to this present convention? In looking at schedule A, which has been the subject of considerable discussion, we find that there are 110 articles on which the duty is considerably less than the duty on similar articles going from the United States. First, on horses, from Canada, the duty is 150 francs; from the United States, 225 francs. On meats of certain kinds, from Canada, 40 francs; from the United States, 60 francs-the same difference on various grades of meat. On fish there is a difference in favour of Canada. On linen yams, from Canada, 80 francs; from the United States, 120 francs. On tools, articles mentioned by the hon. member for Lincoln-spades, scythes, sickles, files, vices, etc., the duty is 140 francs from Canada and 212 from the United States. In another case, 100 francs from Canada; 152 from the United States. And so on through the whole list there are very substantial reductions on behalf of Canada as against similar articles going from the United States-and these are articles made by the hon. member for Lincoln.
The hon. member spoke of buckles; there is a large percentage, as respects the duty, in favour of goods from Canada as against similar goods from the United States. Doors of hardwood or softwood, painted or carved- these are articles made in Canada in large quantities, and the French duty is considerably less on goods coming from Canada tha i it is on goods from the United States. Asbestos is an article which is bought, particularly in the province of Quebec, in very large quantities. On sheets the duty is 67 francs from Canada and 102 francs from the United States; shaped asbestos, 135 francs from Canada and 202 francs from the United States; asbestos threads, 198 francs from Canada and 297 francs from the United States; asbestos plates, 247 francs from Canada and 346 francs from the United States, and so on through the whole list. I find there are at least 110 articles where the duty in favour of Canada is a very large percentage indeed.
Then take schedule B, which hon. gentlemen say is of no use. The right hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen), and the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) alleged that the treaty of 1908 was far and away preferable to the present treaty, but what do we find in looking at the same articles in the treaty of 1908 and the treaty before us at the present time? We find that there are some 800 articles of commerce mentioned in

French Treaty
this treaty affected by the duty on Canadian goods, and on 450 of these the duty is far and away less on Canadian goods going into France by from ten to fifty per cent than it was under the old treaty and on 110 articles from Canada the duts^ is much lower than on the same articles going from the United States. So that it does appear to me that the argument is all in favour of this treaty as against the treaty which was in force for the last fifteen years.
Now it has been alleged and strongly urged by my hon. friend for Lincoln (Mr. Chaplin), also by the right hon. leader of the Opposition as well as the hon. member for West York, that not many of these articles were being exported from Canada to France. I want to tell hon. members of this House that there have been millions of dollars of United States money invested in Canada in manufacturing industries for the sole and only reason that they get the benefit of the Canadian tariff for their export business. I know that because it is happening in the county of Welland, and my hon. friend from Lincoln must know it because the same thing exists in his county. Hundreds of thousands of dollars have been invested in these two counties by United States manufacturing industries for the alleged reason, according to them, that they were getting the benefit of the Canadian tariff for their export business. What do we find under this treaty which this House is not asked to confirm? We find that on 110 articles, practically the necessaries of life, the duty is far and away lower on goods going from Canada than on goods going from the United States. Surely, therefore, we shall have a greater influx of United States money into Canada for the purpose of developing our manufacturing industries. That is what we desire in that section of Canada; that, is what we desire in the whole of Canada.
The first great commercial industry, to call it that, is the farming industry. That is the industry which should be protected, preserved and encouraged more than any other. Our natural resources should be developed and encouraged; our manufacturing industries should be developed and encouraged, and that can . only be done by a sane, sensible tariff policy which exists in my opinion, to the.extent to which it goes, in this very treaty that is now before the House. It is the desire of us all to see Canada prosper, to see our natural resources developed and our manufacturing industries progress, and that can only be done by applying to the industries of
Canada the intelligent, courageous and progressive principles of Liberalism.

Bon.- HUGH GUTHRIE (South Wellington) : Mr. Speaker, I listened with a great deal of interest to the remarks of my hon. friend for Welland (Mr. German), who concluded his address just before the House took recess, and I think I may go so far as to say that the calm, clear, well-reasoned argument which he presented, upon what is really a practical question of trade was in style and tenor very suitable indeed to the occasion and to the question which he sought to argue. While I cannot agree with the conclusion reached by my hon. friend I must say that from his point of view he stated his case with great fairness and with great calmness. He objected, in one instance, to a statement made by my hon. friend for Lincoln (Mr. Chaplin) in regard to the question of the duties upon imported wines, and he seems to take issue upon that question with the attitude adopted by the hon. member for Lincoln some days ago. As both of these hon. members come from what we know as the grape-growing district in the province of Ontario, I think they will have to settle that question pretty much between themselves; at all events I can offer them no light upon the subject. I did gather from the remarks of the Finance Minister, when he originally introduced this matter to the House, that perhaps there was something in the contention of my hon. friend for Lincoln, but that the proper time to correct the error, if there was one, would be upon the presentation of the budget rather than in connection with the present measure.
Apart from that question, my hon. friend for Welland dwelt in his argument almost exclusively upon the fact that in schedule A of the present treaty, likewise in schedule B, certain goods which on export from Canada to
French Treaty

France were formerly at a disanvantage as compared with those of the United States, had now been put upon the same plane as exports from the last-named country; also that in regard to schedule B there will be a large number of reductions from former duties on exports of Canadian goods to France I may tell my hon. friend for Welland that his argument in that respect is not convincing. If the duties to be maintained by France in the future on exports from Canada are yet so high that those goods cannot be profitably exported from this country, the reduction is purely a matter of form and not a matter of substance; it is not a reduction of which we can take any advantage. I tell him also that if he will read over the various items of schedule B to which he referred, he will find instance after instance where the duties which prevail to-day under the treaty of 1908, have been actually increased by the present proposal. I am not persuaded that my hon. friend is right in his conclusion, I take issue with him upon that point; but I must say that he argued the matter very fairly from his point of view.
I think we all realize that the question now before the House is purely a matter of trade and commerce, is purely a business arrangement Whether it be good or whether it be bad for the people of Canada is a question upon which, this House will have to pass; but in my view of the matter nothing is gained by seeking to make it a political question, or treating it from the standpoint of party politics.
I think it is to be regretted that the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Lapointe) . this afternoon became so warm, became as he evidently did so excited, became so over-emphatic, if I may be allowed to use the term, in many of his statements. I think if he had contented himself with a defence of this proposal upon business and economic grounds, and not sought to arouse a storm of partisan enthusiasm from his own side of the House, he would have displayed greater dignity himself and treated the question with more respect. I think his whole statement, this afternoon lacked everything in the nature of sound business argument. I think he absolutely failed to advance sound reasons why this House should adopt this treaty. He referred, of course, to two or three of the minor items which are involved in the present trade proposal. He waxed eloquent upon the question of bronze powders. He waxed eloquent upon the question of fresh or unsalted butter, and had something to say about the statement of my hon. friend for Lincoln (Mr. Chaplin) in

regard to tissues of cotton. I am satisfied, from a re-reading of the speech of my hon. friend for Lincoln upon these three points, that the hon. member was quite correct in the statement which he made to the House. I have Hansard before me. I am not going to refer to it, but any hon. member who desires to verify this statement can find it in the speech of the hon. member for Lincoln a few days ago. But even suppose that on these three points, butter, web cotton and bronze powder, all that the hon. member for Lincoln said was wrong, and all that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Lapointe) said was right, I think that should weigh very very little with this House or any member of it in coming to a conclusion upon the broad question of this treaty. These are matters of but trifling importance. If we are going to arrive at a correct conclusion in regard to this treaty proposal I submit, Mr. Speaker, that it is not altogether out of place to refer very briefly to what one might call the history of the matter. I go back to the year 1894, which is the year during which the first commercial treaty with France was negotiated. Between 1894 and 1908 the trade of this country under the treaty of 1894 did not show any very material gain, either in exports from Canada or in imports into Canada, and I agree with the Finance Minister to-day, who was Finance Minister in 1908, that in the year 1908 the time had arrived for some new arrangement between France and Canada. I was in the House at that time, I supported the treaty, and I am going to give the House a little bit of information on that subject. My right hon. friend and leader (Mr. Meighen) was not in the House in 1908, but in the session of 1909 after he had been elected a member of this House, and when the Finance Minister came before parliament with supplementary legislation to bring into effect the French treaty of 1908, I find in the records of the House, at page 160 of the Votes and Proceedings for the session of 1909-10, the following:
The House then resumed the debate on the proposed motion of Mr. Fielding "That the Bill No. 12 an Act respecting a certain supplementary convention between His Majesty and the President of the French republic be now read a second time."
The question being put on the motion, the House divided, the names were called, they were recorded by the clerk and among those who supported the present Minister of Finance in his motion on that occasion was the right hon. leader of the Opposition. So far as I can remember, the names on the division list, he was the only member of the Opposition at that time who d'd support the Finance

French Treaty
Minister in regard to the French treaty. It is idle at this distance of time for any one to say that my right hon. friend and leader is opposed on principle to a trade arrangement with France. He proved his faith in the matter during the first session he sat in this House, and it is just as idle to say that any member sitting in the official opposition in this House to-day is opposed to any fair and reasonable trade arrangement between Canada and France. We, one and all of us, are in favour of an equitable arrangement for increased trade. What we condemn about the present proposal is that it is too one-sided, that it is not reciprocal, and that there is no mutuality about it, either in advantage or obligation. These are the criticisms we offer against the present proposal, but we are in favour of any reasonable reciprocal trade arrangement that can be made with France.
The treaty of 1908 negotiated by the present Minister of Finance has not finally expired. I know that my hon. friend the Minister of Finance just a few days ago said that that treaty was as dead as Julius Caesar, but I think he rather overstated the fact on that occasion. The treaty is still in existence, as varied by the act of this parliament in 1921, and to-day, on the importation of goods from France into this country, you are bound by the terms of the treaty of 1908, and on the export of goods from this country to France, you are still bound by the terms of that treaty, varied as it was in 1921 by legislation of this parliament. So that it is an existing tariff. arrangement to-day.
There is no doubt that in the month of September 1918, shortly before the end of the war, the government of France adopted a policy of giving notice and denouncing various commercial treaties which France enjoyed throughout the world. France had evidently come to the conclusion that she would make new financial arrangements with the various countries of the world. Notice was given to Canada along with other countries that our treaty would expire within 12 months, which was the time limit required by the treaty. France subsequently gave an intimation, I think by way of withdrawal of the first notice, because for a certain period of time the treaty was carried forward under no very definite arrangement; but in the year 1920, when we in Canada realized that France was reaping no benefit whatever under the treaty of 1908 and that other nations of the world were reaping very substantial benefit under the same treaty, on account of the most favoured nation clause Canada gave notice to France of the termination of the treaty. Then it was that matters were
brought to a head, and negotiations took place which resulted in the agreement known as the modus vivendi agreement, which was ratified in this House on the 15th May, 1921. It is well, though, to remember that in the meantime new arrangements had been consummated by France with the United States. Early in the year 1921 the United States made application to France for more favourable treatment in regard to tariff matters. What the arguments used !by the United States' authorities were we cannot tell. We know what the result was. The result of the representations of the negotiators on behalf of the United States was this: that a much lower tariff was granted by France for a much larger number of articles than the United States had ever enjoyed before, and in many instances these rates were considerably lower than the rates which Canada enjoyed under the French treaty of 1908. That was the situation, which, to say the least of it, was awkward, and I quite realize that as soon as the new government came into power negotiations were commenced, the Finance Minister says, by a visit from the French Consul General of Montreal. Negotiations were, at all events, opened shortly after the new government came into power, with ^ view of making a new trade arrangement to bind both Canada and France for a term of years to come. The new government had not been in power more than a few months when emissaries of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association likewise came to Ottawa and presented a memorial to the Finance Minister showing that, in respect of certain articles, the United States did then enjoy advantages over Canada, so far as Canadian trade with France was concerned. There were, therefore, two reasons to fix these matters in the mind of the Finance Minister. There was the visit from the French Consul General and there was the memorial from the Canadian Manufacturers' Association. Now, an hon. member of this House with the experience in national financing of the present Minister of Finance had distinct notice that, in the very near future treaty negotiations would again be taken up with France with a view to coming to a new trade arrangement. He knew well what the French treaty of 1908 was. He knew what the French present tariff was. He knew the difficulties which would inevitably face him when he went to France to negotiate for a new treaty. He was warned by the Consul General in Montreal and by the Manufacturers' Association, yet he brought down his budget in 1922 and made no preparation whatever in that budget to enable him to conduct successful negotiations with
French Treaty

the government of France. My hon. friend the Finance Minister has informed us that France has a different tariff system from that which we enjoy in Canada. Under the French system he has informed this House that France has adopted a general tariff usually very high, and also a minimum tariff which likewise is pretty high. But there is a large difference between the two tariffs. In many instances one is as much as four times as great as the other, and in some instances five or six times as great. The Finance Minister assured the House that France maintains that particular kind of tariff "as an instrument for commercial negotiation." I think these are his actual worcls. He was fully aware of this last spring before his budget; he knew it when he was called upon by the French Consul General, and it has been well said that to be fore-warned is to be forearmed. He should have armed himself in the 1922 budget, yet, so far as we can judge from the budget which he brought down, he did nothing whatever by way of preparation to meet the situation which he knew must face him in the ensuing months when in consultation with the government of France which possessed under its tariff system this peculiar "instrument for the negotiation of commercial treaties," while he had none. What under such circumstances one might expect to happen did actually happen and the result is the one-sided proposal now before the House.
Before I turn to that point, let me just refer to this other one. I think I am not going beyond the fact in saying that, in the opinion of most people in this country, the results obtained under the international trade treaty between France and Canada of 1908 have fallen far below our expectations. I think in 1908, we all expected that there would be a very substantial increase in the trade between France and Canada as a result of the treaty; but year after year the figures were disappointing. The trade was not being done, and even at the expense of repeating some of the -figures that have been given to the House in the course of this debate, I wish to include in my remarks the actual trade results that were obtained pi-ior to the war under the treaty of 1908.
