Whether or not I should include 1914, is a question. The war broke out in the beginning of August, 1914, after only four months of our financial year had elapsed, so that it may be said that eight months of that year were war months. But taking the whole six years from 1909 to 1914, both inclusive, we find that we bought from France under the treaty of 1908, 871,264,000 worth of goods, and France purchased from us only $14,514,000 worth. Therefore, in those six years there was an adverse balance of trade of $57,000,000 against Canada. I am going to omit the war years in the statement that I submit to the House. I come from 1914 down to the year 1922, which is the last year for which I have been able to get complete trade reports. For 1922, I find that we bought from France $13,500,000 worth of goods, and France bought from us $8,208,000 worth. But we had a statement made in the House to-day of the trade returns for the first eleven months of the last complete year, or up to the first March of the present year, and as I recollect the figures given by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Lapointe) this afternoon, our exports to France had reached a total of about $12,000,000, while our imports from France during the same eleven months had come down to $11,000,000. I think that I have learned the reason for this. We know that there are monthly as well as yearly reports from the Trade and Commerce department. It so happens that last year we had a very heavy crop of wheat in this country, and, I regret to say there was a very low price for wheat. France, on the other hand, was in the market to buy wheat, and I have been informed that wheat comprises three million dollars of the increase in our exports to France during the last eleven months. During the previous year our exports of wheat to France amounted to about $1,250,000, while for 11 months of this year they have increased to $4,000,000 worth or thereabouts. The other notable increase in the present year has been in sugar. During the last eleven months there is an increase of just about $1,000,000 worth of sugar.
I mention these two matters particularly because the treaty does not affect either of them one way or the other. They are both under the French maximum or general tariff, and I suppose you might say also that they are both under the French minimum tariff, because the rate upon them is precisely the

French Treaty
same under both the general and the minimum tariffs. Under the general tariff the rate on wheat, is 7 francs per 100 kilograms and under the minimum tariff the rate is precisely the same. Under the general tariff the rate on sugar is 90 francs per 100 kilograms, and under the minimum tariff the rate is precisely the same. Therefore, importations or exportations of both these commodities are unaffected by either the present proposal or by the treaty of 1908, because the rate under the general and the minimum tariff is the same. Whether you have a treaty or not does not matter as regards exports of wheat and sugar to Prance, because the rates are the same to us and all the rest of the world, no advantage being given to any nation.
There are however certain aspects of the present treaty which call, I think, for more than passing comment, particularly when one seeks to make a comparison between the arrangement contained in the proposal now before the House and the arrangement which the Minister of Finance made in 1908, and which this parliament ratified. I point out in the first instance, that whenever you find a variation between the trade arrangement of 1908 and the present proposal, you find it is in the interest of France and to the disadvantage of Canada. It is significant that every variation that occurs is in the same direction-an enlargement of the liberty of action of France, a contraction or restriction of the rights of Canada. I cannot find a single variation in the terms of the two treaties which is not favourable to France and at the same time a limitation upon Canada. I take for example the goods referred to in schedule A of the present proposal. These are goods which under the proposal are entitled to entry into France at the minimum French tariff. I compare article 1 and article 2 of the present proposal with the same articles in the treaty of 1908, and I find this marked distinction. Under the treaty of 1908 we not only had the right to ship our products into France at minimum tariff rates but also into all the French colonies, protectorates and possessions. That has been altered. The present arrangement permits us to ship goods under schedule A to French colonies, possessions and protectorates "having the same customs tariff as France." These words were not in the former treaty. Consequently if a possession of France has a different tariff-and I assume for reasons that I will state in a moment that many of them have-we have no right to export to that possession or colony upon the same basis as we are entitled to deal with France herself.
In the next place, by article 2 of the present tariff France grants her minimum tariff to Canada as one of the most favoured nations. We are guaranteed most favoured nation treatment, according to article 2. That is not the way the former treaty was settled; the treaty of 1908 expressly provided that if France made a better arrangement with any "foreign country"-not the most favoured nation-Canada should have the benefit of such arrangement-. I am fully aware that there are eleven nations in the world at this time who, as respects Canada and France, are entitled to what is called most favoured nation treatment; but there are a good many more than eleven important trading nations in the world. Under the treaty of 1908 we were entitled to the ben-:-fiit of any tariff that France granted " to any foreign country "; under this proposal we come in only for the treatment accorded to the eleven most favoured nations.
Under the treaty of 1908 France likewise reserved a small zone for tariff administration purposes as between herself and border states. Article II of the old treaty reads:
The privileges which have been or may be granted to border states for facilitating frontier traffic within a limit not exceeding 15 kilometres on each side of the boundary.
That provision has been very much enlarged under the present proposal, which provides that France may make any tariff arrangement she sees fit with "border states," which means with Spain, with Italy, with Switzerland, with Belgium or with Germany, and Canada cannot claim the benefit of any such arrangement This is an express reservation by France in so many words, so plain that he who runs may read. And likewise France has insisted on another condition for her own benefit over and above anything she asked of Canada in 1908; that is, her right to make special trade treaties with states or countries with which she has been at war, which would of course include Germany, Austria, Turkey and Bulgaria.
Now, I think France has pretty well provided in this treaty that she is to be at liberty to make practically any trade arrangements she likes with pretty much any country in Europe without our being able to take advantage of it. This applies to schedule A.
Well, what is the proposal in regard to schedule B? This schedule represents those goods which, if this treaty be ratified, will be entitled to go into France from Canada at a percentage of reduction as between the general tariff and the minimum tariff of France. Perhaps an example is the best way of illustrating the operation of this provision. Supposing the general tariff in France is 200 francs
French Treaty

on an article and the minimum tariff is 100 francs, and the percentage of reduction in favour of Canada is 50 per cent; the difference between the general and the minimum tariff being 100 francs, 50 per cent of that would be 50 francs. Take 50 from the 200 francs, the general tariff, and the net tariff on Canadian goods would be 150 francs.
With such terms in a treaty is it not of vital importance to Canada that the proportion as between the general and the minimum tariff should always remain unchanged? But France has taken special pains to express clearly in this treaty that she is not to be bound by such a provision; on the contrary France has reserved expressly to herself the right to raise her maximum or her minimum tariff, or both, just as she may deem proper, but all Canada will get is the benefit of a percentage of reduction as between the general and minimum tariffs. Suppose in the case I have just put that the day after this treaty is ratified by this parliament France for her own purposes increases her general tariff to 400 francs, what is the result? The difference between this tariff and the minimum would then be 300 franck, and our percentage of reduction would be 50 per cent of the difference, or 150 francs. Deduct this from the 400 francs, which is the general tariff, and the rate on the goods of this country entering France would be 250 francs instead of the rate of 150 francs which I quoted a few minutes ago. And France reserves the right to make such increases as and when she may so desire.
France was quite justified in making the best bargain she could. Nobody can complain of that. In fact this afternoon I was rather surprised when the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Lapointe) hinted that somebody in this quarter of the House had suggested that the negotiators for France had acted in some respects unfairly in the negotiations. No such suggestion was made from this cfuarter. We are prepared to pay the negotiators for France in this matter every compliment. They are entitled to it. They certainly were wide-awake when they negotiated this treaty. I do not think they have missed much-indeed, I do not think they have missed anything. The treaty appears to be all in favour of France; every fresh limitation, every new condition has given an additional advantage to France and imposed a corresponding disadvantage upon Canada. The French diplomats have certainly made a splendid bargain for France.
In regard to goods in schedule B the position is simply this: France may alter the

rates of duty upon these goods to-morrow and most effectually exclude us from her markets. Does anyone think we are entitled to the" most favoured nation treatment with respect to goods mentioned in schedule B? Indeed we are not; France has reserved that point too. In the treaty of 1908 it is provided that we shall have the benefit of the lowest French tariff with any foreign nation; but when we come to schedule B of the present treaty it merely says that we shall get the benefit of the lowest rate accorded to the United States. Other nations may enjoy much lower rates; all we get in regard to goods on schedule B is the lowest rate which is given to the United States.
Then there is another provision just as favourable to France as schedules A and B. In respect of goods that are not in either schedule A or schedule B we simply get the United States rate, and if the agreement between France and the United States shall at any time be terminated, then we get a 25 per cent reduction and the difference between the general and the minimum French rates. But there is a curious provision in repect to the goods not included in schedules A or B, and that provision is contained in article V. It says:
If at any time France grants to the United States of America for any products other than those enumerated in schedules A and B to this convention more favourable treatment than is granted to Canada, Canada shall be entitled to claim the benefit of the same treatment for any identical or similar products originating in and coming from Canada, on condition that France shall be entitled to ask from Canada a reasonable and equivalent concession.
When France deals with our diplomats; when France deals with the two ministers of this government who went to Paris to negotiate this treaty, France expressly provides that if any concession is granted to Canada, Canada shall grant an identical concession to France. But when the negotiators for the United States went over in 1921 to . arrange their trade convention, for aught we know or are able to learn about the matter they gave no concession whatever to France and France gave them freely what they asked. But under the present treaty, even if in the future the United States gets a further concession of which we claim the benefit, we are bound under the treaty to give a'similar concession to France.
Now, my summary of the agreement as it is presented to parliament is that it is by no means as satisfactory a treaty as that which is still in force. Every change has been a disadvantage to this country. France has succeeded in securing for herself absolute freedom

French Treaty
223;
of action for the future; Canada, on the other hand, is bound under the hard and fast terms of express stipulations. Let me turn for a moment to the provisions in regard to Canada. Canada in respect to schedule D grants to France a fixed rate of duty; if the bill is passed bringing this treaty into force we absolutely fix the rates of duty on all the goods mentioned in schedule D coming from France to Canada and we cannot alter these rates unless we denounce the treaty. We have agreed to it; we have allowed ourselves no liberty of action; we cannot change a single rate under schedule D-that is the express language of the treaty. Then, in regard to schedule E which is a list of goods in respect of which Canada says to France, "We will give you the intermediate tariff of Canada and in addition we will give you a discount of 10 per cent." One would think that was a pretty reasonable offer to France and that as France herself had retained liberty of action in almost every respect she would have granted Canada some liberty of action; that some reciprocal arrangement would have been effected. But no, the negotiators for France say, "You must bind yourselves that you will always maintain the same proportion between the intermediate and the general tariff of Canada." We cannot alter this proportion. We can raise the general tariff, it is true, but if we do we must keep up the same proportion between our general and our intermediate tariffs so that a 10 per cent advantage to France will be sure to result. If there were anything like mutuality in this bargain, anything like reciprocal treatment, surely France would not have insisted on her right to raise her minimum or general tariff, one or the other or both, as she saw fit, and would not have so far bound the hands of the Canadian representatives as to schedule D to say, "These are the figures and you cannot alter them; you shall go no higher or no lower," and as to schedule E to say, "We will have your intermediate tariff with 10 per cent off, but you must bind yourselves to keep up the same proportion between your intermediate and your general tariff as at the present time." So again with schedule F, which deals with goods which France will be entitled to send into Canada at a discount of 15 per cent from the intermediate tariff. The same language is employed in schedule F as in schedule E; we cannot change the proportion of our general and our intermediate tariff in any way.
I have tried to state these things as clearly and as fairly as I can. I have tried to point out to the House the tremendous difference
which exists between these two treaties, that of 1908 and the one now offered by the Finance Minister for the ratification of this parliament. If our trade did not succeed very well under the treaty of 1908; if we were disappointed in the trade results under that treaty-and I think we all were-what will happen to us under a treaty so overbalanced in favour of France as the present proposal? Every restriction in favour of France, every variation, every liberty, we are bound to by the treaty, and France is perfectly free to alter it or to nullify it as she sees fit. That is one aspect of the matter which appeals to me. But there is another important phase of the matter and even at the risk of some repetition I am going to refer to it.
My hon. friend the Minister of Finance very candidly states that in his opinion this trade arrangement is of far more consequence to Canada than it is to France. I entirely differ from him in that opinion. He has pointed out the enormous difference between the French general and minimum tariffs and the comparatively small difference between our * intermediate and general tariffs. He says that in one case the general tariff of France may be four or five times the minimum tariff while in Canada the difference is not more than perhaps five or seven and a half per cent between our general and intermediate rates and that is true. But I judge of the matter from the actual trade returns. If France sold to Canada last year $13,500,000 worth of goods and Canada sold to France a little over $8,000,000 worth of goods might one not assume that the trade as between the two countries is substantially more valuable and important to France than it is to Canada? What do the trade figures disclose? I will take the figures submitted to-day by my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries for the eleven months of the present year-$12,000,000 of exports from Canada to France. I received to-day from the Department of Trade and Commerce a statement of the total exports of Canada for the last year and I find that the domestic merchandise exported ran to the enormous sum of $932,000,000 odd. Of that, $12,000,000 went to France, about one and one-quarter per [DOT] cent of our exports. Is the export to France, then, such a vital matter to Canada as my hon. friend the Minister of Finance seems to think? I do not regard it as such a vital matter at all; if we had no trade treaty between France and Canada to-day I do not believe it would prove such a calamity that we need fear. It would not even seriously injure us. I do believe it would be a commercial misfortune. I think what we

I do want a fair and reasonable commercial arrangement between Canada and France and every one on this side of the House wants it also. We desire any kind of a reciprocal arrangement with France which will confer something like equal benefits upon both countries, but the arrangement which is proposed by the government is so one-sided, so overbalanced, and so unequal in every respect, so far as I have been able

to examine it, that in my opinion this House would not be warranted in accepting it as a satisfactory trade agreement between the two countries.
It would be far better for the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) to drop this proposal. It would be far better for him and his colleague to go back and try again. They know something of the game of treaty-making now. Let them take a little longer time, if necessary, and let them say to the negotiators of France: " In the bright light of an April daj this proposal does not suit the parliament of Canada. It insists upon a better bargain ". To whose interest is it most to make a treaty? As I said before, it is certainly to the interest of France, and I have no doubt, if this government should persist, it can procure a less objectionable treaty. The United States certainly secured a better one, and if our negotiators were as persistent, patient and diplomatic as those able statesmen whom France designated to conduct its side of the negotiations, I think we might have secured a much more satisfactory treaty than the one now before us.
I have tried to balance the advantages and disadvantages under this arrangement. I have tried to make some kind of an estimate of what we may reasonably expect in the way of increased trade, although that is very hard to estimate. I have mentioned several lines in which I think it may be possible to increase our exports to France; but after all, what will this amount to? Perhaps a million, two million, think you, three million a year in increased exports? Less than half of that, I feel sure. Suppose our exports should increase by two or three million dollars; last year the total amount was only eight million dollars odd all told, of agricultural products, manufactured products and everything else. Suppose the increase in exports is say thre ; million dollars per annum, are we not paying too much for such an increase in export trade? Are we not tying our hands so completely under this agreement that we will not be able in the future to take advantage of more favourable arrangements which may be offered other countries of the world? Are wre not going to pay too highly by loss to our treasury of $850,000 a year for the little bit of benefit which may possibly result? But apart from that altogether, are we not by this very treaty, granting favours, by reduction of taxation, to the people who least require such reductions? What satisfaction is it to the general public of Canada to know that a few of the people in the cities of this country are going to get their luxuries, their silks, their laces and their

French Treaty
wines under a duty of $27 a hundred instead of $30 as formerly? We may find it very hard to explain this aspect to the people if this treaty should go through. It will be of no benefit to the people in my constituency. It may be of some little benefit to the rich people of Montreal, Toronto or other large centres of population who purchase luxuries. But perhaps the worst feature of the question is that the loss of revenue must be made up, and as you cannot make up this loss by increased taxation on luxuries, because your treaty forbids it-consequently it must be made up by further taxation of the necessaries of life. These are the reasons why this treaty does not commend itself to me. It is for those reasons that I was prepared to move an amendment upon the second reading of this bill; but during the dinner recess, I may tell the House that I was in consultation with my leader, and he thinks it better that the bill should go into committee and be fully discussed there. I certainly intend, however, to reserve my right on the third reading of the bill to move the amendment which I had proposed to move to-night, but which I am dissuaded from doing by the request of my leader. Perhaps, on the whole, when the bill is discussed in committee, we may be able to demonstrate more clearly than we are able to do now, that the proposal is not to the advantage or benefit of the great mass of the people of this country.

They say that if you want to have a friend, you must be one, and I would advise one who wants to see the world look good-natured, to try and be good-natured himself. If he has that party rancour that turns to gall and that turns the milk of human kindness sour, for heaven's sake, let him pluck it from him and cast it away. As long as I have the honour of being a member of this House and indeed, as long as I have the privilege of living in this country and can raise my voice, I always want to be able to feel a sympathetic chord vibrate in my heart when I see a good Canadian, moved by high motives of public duty, leave the comforts of his home and family, go over to another country, and stay there patiently for months working and negotiating to do something for his native land. I want always to be able to applaud that man. That is what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) has done, and he should receive the thanks of this House and this country. Sitting in this House as we are, making a treaty with France, we can always make a bargain very easily until we 
meet, the other man with whom we have to deal. Hon. members have sat in this House and made a treaty with France without having any French representatives present. Hon. members have compared duties under the trade agreement which has been denounced, which duties, therefore, do not exist, with the duties which obtain under this treaty. That is manifestly unjust and unfair. I regret that men should depart from the plain path of honesty, rectitude and justice in order to belittle a great work that one of their fellow countrymen has succeeded in accomplishing.

He said that in a tone of scorn as though the Minister of Finance was not the solemnly accredited representative of the Canadian people and responsible to them, but rather as though the minister were his own hired man. But, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance did not answer that poser, and I suppose it will stand until there shall be no more sea for Canadian delegates to cross in an endeavour to negotiate trade treaties with any foreign people, whether those delegates be as wise as gods, or whether they have all the simplicity which the hon. member for Lincoln and a few of his associates who have spoken in this debate would evidently relate to the present Canadian negotiators. I must congratulate the hon. member for Lincoln upon the vast amount of work which he undertook in giving item by item the schedules of this treaty. I cannot congratulate him upon the use he made of his very laboriously obtained facts.
Another hon. gentleman who spoke in this debate assumed an easier air, an attitude more offhand, more debonair, more cavalier even than any other debater on that side. I refer to the gay and hon. ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton). He was in- * sistent that these two hon. and distinguished negotiators on behalf of Canada had acted not only like schoolboys, but I think he classed their actions as being those only of idiots or lunatics. He asked, with an air of bravado: "Why did you not hire a good Yankee to negotiate this treaty for you?" Well, Mr. Speaker, he did not suggest any American name, but I was just wondering whether we could not again have hired the Griffenhagens. I will say this: If they were rewarded for their disservice toward Canada we should easily have found them out of a job and very glad to be hired again and to accept a few more hundred thousand dollars of Canadian money.
Then the hon. member reached the climax when he used the word "gullible" as applying to these two ministers.
Mr. Speaker, I have about concluded. It is so late that I shall not go further down the few notes I did take. But seriously I do not think this House is treated writh common courtesy when certain members on the opposition side would have it appear that the two distinguished, experienced, able and patriotic delegates who negotiated inis treaty were over in France, not to study what they could get, not to see how little France would take in the arrangement of a treaty that would be worth something to us. I think this House will regard it as an axiom that these two hon. TMr. Putnam.]
gentlemen had the motive of getting as good a bargain as they could for Canada: that having arrived there, their first step would be to make discreet investigation as to what tariff concessions France would make to Canada, and, in turn, what would be the minimum tariff concessions France might exact and expect from Canada. I have no doubt that they proceeded on that basis. I listened to the speeches of those two hon. ministers, and I saw not one symptom that they had Defrayed their trust, or that they had not done the best they could and the best that could be done. I was delighted to be confirmed in that elementary opinion by the hon. leader of the Progressives (Mr. Forke) who admitted that while the treaty was not anything like as long a step as he would desire in the right direction, it had merit; that it was good as far as it went, and he did give the hon. gentlemen who negotiated it the credit of having, on the very face of things, done the best they could. But when the question comes to a vote I want hon. members to weigh the utter absurdity of the attitude taken by some hon. members who stand up dnd either throw out the implication or make the direct statement that these two negotiators could easily have got more for the very asking. That sort of thing is simply a waste of words. They are words not budded into the order of any edifice; they are words, Mr. Speaker, which fall as far short of the goal of proof as though they had been left unsaid.

speechtext: No words of mine are necessary on seconding the motion. This country not only entertains a feeling of profound devotion to the Empire, but has the highest regard personally, and in every way, for the Royal family. The happy event of to-day may well indeed be followed by a message of congratulation from the House.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION OF CONGRATULATION ON WEDDING OF THEIR ROYAL HIGHNESSES
speechtext: I would like to say a few words in support of this motion. I have had a rather long experience and am perhaps in a better position to express an opinion on the subject than the Prime Minister or the leader of the Opposition. I wish to congratulate His Royal Highness upon the fact that he has taken a Scotch lassie. Should there be any doubts about his happiness they can in view of that fact be dismissed at once. He will have a happy life, but I cannot prophesy as to the length of it. However, I join with my right hon. friends in wishing their Royal Highnesses long life and much happiness.
Motion agreed to.
